Stricture Urethra India

Urethral stricture disease: what it is and how it is treated

A plain-language guide for patients from Dr. Bokka Sri Harsha, Consultant Urologist specialising in urethroplasty and reconstructive urology. Read it before your visit, and bring your questions.

Your surgeon

Dr. Bokka Sri Harsha is a Consultant Urologist, Robotic Surgeon and Andrologist in Hyderabad. He holds an MCh in Urology from JIPMER and trained at JIPMER, Pondicherry and Tata Memorial Hospital, Mumbai.

He performs urethroplasty, including buccal mucosa graft and anastomotic repair, for patients with urethral stricture. He has more than 20 publications and has received awards at national conferences.

The problem

The urethra is the tube that carries urine from the bladder out of the body. A urethral stricture is a segment of that tube that has become narrowed by scar tissue. The scar forms in and around the spongy tissue that surrounds the urethra (spongiofibrosis), so the channel becomes tight and rigid and urine cannot pass freely.

Strictures are most common in men, because the male urethra is long. Strictures can be short or long, single or multiple, and can occur anywhere from the bladder outlet to the tip of the penis. Their location and length largely decide which treatment works best.

Common symptoms

  • A weak, slow or splitting urine stream
  • Straining to pass urine, or a stream that stops and starts
  • Feeling that the bladder has not emptied fully
  • Needing to pass urine often, or dribbling after you finish
  • Repeated urinary tract infections
  • Inability to pass urine at all (urinary retention), which is an emergency

How it is diagnosed

Your urologist will ask about your history and may use a urine flow test, an ultrasound scan of the bladder after voiding, an X-ray dye study of the urethra (urethrogram), and a flexible camera examination (urethroscopy or cystoscopy). These show where the stricture is, how long it is and how dense the scar is.

The burden

A stricture is more than a slow stream. Because scar tissue tends to return, many people live with it for years, and it affects daily life in several ways.

Physical

  • Repeated infections of the bladder, prostate or kidneys
  • Bladder stones and a thickened, weakened bladder
  • Urinary retention and the need for a catheter
  • In severe or long-standing cases, back-pressure that can harm the kidneys

Daily life and wellbeing

  • Time spent planning around toilets, and disturbed sleep
  • Anxiety about sudden retention
  • Effects on sexual function and confidence
  • Loss of work time

Treatment cycle

  • Repeated dilations or urethrotomies, each with a risk of recurrence and a cost
  • Repeated visits, tests and antibiotic courses
  • Uncertainty about whether it will come back

Being told your options early, and understanding which treatments offer a lasting cure, can spare you years of repeated procedures.

Risk factors

Some strictures have a clear cause. In others no cause is found (idiopathic). The main known causes are:

Injury to the urethra

  • A fall astride (straddle injury) or a blow to the perineum
  • Pelvic fracture

Medical instrumentation

  • Prolonged or traumatic catheter use
  • Prostate or bladder surgery through the urethra (for example TURP)
  • Cystoscopy and other endoscopic procedures
  • Previous hypospadias repair

Inflammation and infection

  • Lichen sclerosus (also called BXO), a chronic skin condition that can involve the urethra
  • Sexually transmitted infections such as gonorrhoea, and other urethritis

Other

  • Radiation to the pelvis or prostate
  • Older age, and conditions that slow healing such as diabetes or smoking

Prevention starts with avoiding unnecessary catheters, choosing correctly sized catheters, and getting infections treated early.

Surgical options

Treatments fall into two groups: those that open the stricture from inside, and those that remove or rebuild the scarred segment (urethroplasty). Your best option depends on the stricture's length, location, cause and how many treatments you have already had.

OptionWhat it involvesBest suited toApproximate long-term success
DilationGradually stretching the narrowing with graded instrumentsTemporary relief, or when surgery is not suitableLow; scar usually returns
Internal urethrotomy (DVIU)A small blade or laser cuts the scar under camera guidanceA first, short (under 2 cm) bulbar strictureAbout half of first-time cases; falls with each repeat
Excision and end-to-end repair (anastomotic urethroplasty)The scarred segment is removed and the healthy ends are joinedShort bulbar strictures, and pelvic fracture injuriesAround 90 to 95 percent
Substitution urethroplastyThe narrowed area is widened with a patch graft, usually from inside the cheek (buccal mucosa)Longer strictures, and penile urethraAround 80 to 90 percent
Staged urethroplastyReconstruction in two operations, several months apartComplex, long or previously failed casesVaries with complexity
Perineal urethrostomyA permanent new opening below the scrotum, so urine passes sitting downWhen reconstruction is not possible or not wantedReliable for urine drainage
Why repeated urethrotomy is discouraged. If a stricture returns after a first urethrotomy, further cutting or dilation seldom cures it and each round can lengthen the scar. Guidelines generally suggest considering urethroplasty after one or two failed attempts.

Success rates: urethroplasty compared with urethrotomy (DVIU)

Success means the stricture stays open, with a good stream and no further procedures. The bars show typical ranges reported in published studies.

Urethroplasty, overall85 to 95%
End-to-end repair, short bulbar stricture90 to 95%
Buccal mucosa graft urethroplasty80 to 90%
Urethrotomy (DVIU), first treatment of a short stricture50 to 60%
Urethrotomy (DVIU), second or later treatment20 to 30%

Urethroplasty results tend to hold for many years. Urethrotomy results fade over time, and most recurrences appear within the first one to two years. This is why urethroplasty is usually advised for strictures that come back, for longer strictures, and for strictures after infection or injury. Ranges vary with stricture length, location, cause and surgeon experience, and your own result cannot be predicted from an average.

Success figures are approximate and depend on the surgeon's experience, the cause and the stricture. Ask your surgeon about their own results.

Managing the stricture until surgery

Some patients need a temporary catheter through the abdomen (suprapubic catheter) to drain the bladder safely while waiting. Some are taught self-catheterization or self-dilation to keep the channel open.

Complications and how they are managed

Every operation carries risks. Most of the following are uncommon or temporary. Tap each one to read more.

Stricture recurrence

The stricture can come back, most often within the first two years after any procedure.

Management: follow-up with flow tests and, if needed, a camera check. A recurrence may be treated with a repeat urethroplasty or, for a short web-like narrowing, a limited urethrotomy. Report any weakening of your stream promptly.

Infection and wound problems

Urinary infection, or infection or bruising of the perineal wound, can happen.

Management: antibiotics, wound care and drainage of any collection. Preventive antibiotics are commonly given around surgery.

Bleeding

Blood in the urine is common for days after an endoscopic procedure or urethroplasty. Heavier bleeding is rare.

Management: fluids and rest usually suffice. Bleeding that forms clots or blocks urine needs prompt medical review.

Dribbling after urination

Urine that leaks a few drops after you finish is a common effect of bulbar urethroplasty.

Management: after you pass urine, press firmly behind the scrotum and squeeze along the urethra toward the tip ("milking"), and wait a moment before leaving the toilet. It often improves over months.

Erection and ejaculation changes

Temporary softer erections or reduced ejaculatory force can follow surgery, usually improving in weeks to months. Lasting erectile dysfunction is uncommon after most anterior urethroplasties, but is more likely after pelvic fracture repair.

Management: reassurance, time, and treatment for erectile dysfunction if it persists. Tell your surgeon about baseline sexual function before surgery.

Penile curvature, shortening or skin problems

Repairs on the penile urethra can occasionally cause bending or a sense of shortening, or skin swelling.

Management: most settle with healing. Persistent bend may need further evaluation and surgery.

Fistula or urine leak

Rarely, an abnormal channel or leak develops at the repair.

Management: catheter drainage to let the area heal, and repair surgery if it persists. A dye X-ray is usually done before the catheter is removed to check the repair has healed.

Mouth graft site problems (buccal mucosa)

Numbness, tightness, mild pain, altered salivation or a reduced ability to open the mouth widely can follow cheek graft harvest. Most improve with time.

Management: gentle jaw-stretching exercises and pain relief. The cheek heals without stitches or with dissolving stitches in most cases.

Leakage of urine (incontinence), after posterior repairs

Repairs close to the bladder neck, such as for pelvic fracture injuries or after prostate treatment, carry a risk of leakage.

Management: pelvic floor exercises, and if needed, an artificial urinary sphincter or sling.

Positioning injuries and general surgical risks

Long operations in the lithotomy position can rarely cause temporary leg numbness or pressure injuries. General anaesthetic and clot risks apply.

Management: careful padding and positioning by the team, early walking after surgery, and clot prevention measures.

Seek urgent help if you cannot pass urine, have fever with chills, heavy bleeding or clots, or increasing pain or swelling after surgery.

In the operating room and the classroom

Reconstructive surgery, robotic surgery and teaching are all part of the care you receive.
